one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.7x fair value. Interesting below about $79.

profile.what: Morgan Stanley is a global investment bank and one of the largest wealth managers in the world, after acquiring Smith Barney, E*Trade and Eaton Vance.
profile.money: Wealth and investment management now earns roughly half of revenue from steady fees on client assets. The rest is investment banking and trading, which swing with markets.
profile.valued: Valued on P/E and price to book. Morgan Stanley earns a higher multiple than pure investment banks because recurring wealth-management fees make earnings more stable.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: An investment bank made steadier by one of the largest wealth-management businesses.
risks: Still exposed to trading and deal cycles.

meaning.what_it_does: A wealth manager and investment bank.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Fees on client assets, plus investment-banking and trading revenue.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Trillions of dollars of sticky client assets generate steady fees.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A long bear market shrinks fee-earning assets.

moat.summary: The wealth-management business is far steadier than traditional investment banking.

industry.summary: Banking changes slowly, but results depend on credit cycles and interest rates.

management.summary: The shift toward wealth management has made earnings more durable.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 13.3% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 1.29–1.71 × book value per share of $74.80.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $74.80 × 1.29–1.71. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
